questions.question: What is MCP primarily for?
options: Training language models from scratch.
Replacing HTTP with a new network protocol.
Standardizing AI client-server access to tools and context.
Encrypting local files.
questions.explanation: MCP defines a standard protocol so any AI assistant can connect to any MCP server to access tools, resources, and prompt templates without custom integration code for each pairing.

questions.question: Which mapping is correct in MCP?
options: Tool -> data, Resource -> action, Prompt -> database table.
Tool -> action, Resource -> readable data, Prompt -> reusable template.
Tool -> model, Resource -> API key, Prompt -> shell command.
All three mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: MCP defines three distinct capability types: tools are callable actions, resources are readable data sources, and prompts are reusable templates — conflating them leads to poor server design.

questions.question: Why should clients perform capability discovery?
options: To disable permission checks.
To avoid logging requests.
Because discovery is required only for frontend apps.
Because available capabilities can vary by server/environment.
questions.explanation: Different MCP servers expose different tools and resources; a client that hardcodes capability names instead of discovering them at runtime will break when the server configuration changes.

questions.question: What is least privilege in MCP server design?
options: Expose only the minimum capabilities required for the task.
Disable all validation.
Give admin access to every tool by default.
Use only read-only prompts and no tools.
questions.explanation: Exposing only the capabilities a client actually needs limits the damage if a tool is called with bad arguments or if the model makes an incorrect decision about which action to take.

questions.question: What should happen before executing a tool call?
options: Execute first, validate after.
Validate call shape and required arguments.
Skip validation for trusted users.
Convert all arguments to strings.
questions.explanation: Validating the call shape and required argument types before execution catches model mistakes early; executing first and validating after means side effects have already occurred when you discover the problem.

questions.question: Why are audit logs important for MCP operations?
options: They speed up embeddings.
They replace permission policies.
They remove the need for tests.
They provide traceability for who called what and with what result.
questions.explanation: Audit logs record every tool call, its arguments, and its result so you can reconstruct what the model did during an incident, verify compliance, and debug unexpected behavior.

questions.question: What is a safer rollout strategy for new MCP servers?
options: Disable logs until production.
Expose all actions immediately for faster iteration.
Start read-only, then add guarded write actions with approval gates.
Skip schema design and rely on model intuition.
questions.explanation: Starting with read-only tools lets you verify discovery, authentication, and logging before you expose actions with side effects; approval gates on write actions add a human checkpoint for high-risk operations.

questions.question: What does a clean MCP separation improve the most?
options: Maintainability and interoperability across hosts and tools.
Filesystem throughput.
GPU memory usage.
SQL query planning.
questions.explanation: When tools, resources, and prompts have clear boundaries and well-defined schemas, any compliant host can connect to the server and teams can maintain or replace individual capabilities without touching the rest.
